lines.note: Idaxi means taking or putting out, with the historical aita principal part retained. The scan begins with capital I; Su starts an example divided across the next line.

ſono completes Suſono; chiuo idaſu means drawing blood. The Portuguese identifies the application as bleeding horses, so the veterinary context is retained without forcing an uncertain modern identification of Suſo.
Idaxiauaxe means causing contributions or forces to come out from both sides. The faint initial I is restored; the Portuguese construction continues below.
Both sides are involved. Caneuo idaxi begins an example of putting up money jointly, with the compound verb continued on the next row.
Auaxete completes idaxi auaxete; aqinaiuo ſuru describes trading together. The Portuguese begins the equivalent mercantile explanation.

runs.text: de companhia tirando, & pondo dinheiro de

lines.note: The trade is conducted in partnership, with money put forward. The final de introduces the parties contributing it.
The money comes from one side and the other. Riǒgin tagaini begins a second example involving the two opposing military camps.
Both camps bring out hidden troops and make them fight one another. The printed tatacauaximu preserves the historical causative construction and is not modernized.

runs.text: Dambos os arrayais deitando a gente fora q̃ eſta

lines.note: The Portuguese says that both camps brought out the troops who had been concealed. The scan supports Dambos with b, not OCR Damhos; eſta continues below without an added hyphen.
Ua completes eſtaua; the troops had been hidden in the field and fought. The opening vowel of eſcondida is e, not the OCR's o.

Ide is an interjection, glossed Eya or òraſus, an exhortation rather than the following verb meaning to go out. The enlarged detail confirms a grave stroke over ò, so retain the aligned reading; the example begins Ide mo- with a printed hyphen.

runs.text: Ora dexaime que eu vos darei

lines.note: No completes mono; Ide mono mixô introduces an emphatic challenge. The Portuguese paraphrases it as 'now let me, and I shall give you ...', continued below.
Hũas poucas completes the idiomatic threat of giving someone a few blows or a dressing-down; the gloss leaves the precise object unstated with &c.
This Ide is the verb for going out, glossed Sair. All of the Japanese headword is upright; the draft's italic d is a type-classification error.
The noun Ide denotes coming or going out, glossed as vinda or ſaida. It is separate from the verbal principal-parts entries around it.
The next Ide means boiling or cooking food, distinguished from going out by its Portuguese gloss. Its printed principal parts are retained despite the homography.
Ideai means meeting someone while going out. The marked principal parts are retained; the example follows below.
Qiacujinni ideyǒ illustrates going out to meet guests. The Portuguese Saindo encontrar continues into the object on the next row.
Com oshoſpedes completes the guest-meeting example. The close printed joining of os and hoſpedes is retained from the aligned draft.
Idebune is a vessel going out or departing. The gloss describes its motion rather than a special kind of boat.
Ideiri means going out and coming in. The principal part is iru with r, not OCR ixu; it corresponds to the entering element in this compound.
The noun Ideiri denotes entrance and departure. Its lack of principal parts distinguishes it from the preceding verbal entry.
Idemucai is going out to meet someone. The Portuguese confirms the outward meeting action rather than a stationary encounter.
Ideqi describes something happening or arising. The explanation's subject, algũa couſa, is supplied by the following row.
Algũa couſa completes the gloss as something arising or occurring. The short row closes this verb entry.
Ideqitari means coming or issuing forth. The scan supports t in the kitari element, not OCR c; Mia- begins Miaco in the example below.
Cono completes Miacono; the example says fire came from the southeast of the capital. Retain the historical fi and the printed ideqitatte form.

runs.text: parte do leſte, & ſul do Miaco vinha o

lines.note: The Portuguese specifies the east-and-south side of Miaco as the fire's origin. Miaco is a Japanese place-name embedded in this Portuguese explanation and is flagged for whole-word typeface review.
Fogo supplies the fire that arose. Its first letter is f, not OCR long ſ, and final S is the upright written-register label.
Idetachi means dressing or arraying oneself neatly. The Portuguese elaborates the manner on the next row.
Polidamente completes the description as dressing elegantly or neatly. It is the adverb governing the preceding verbs.
The noun Idetachi denotes attire or arrangement of clothing. The scan supports the fully italic word Atauio, correcting both the draft's letter sequence and its spurious internal font changes.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Comer no tempo que ſe partem pera

lines.note: The paragraph introduces a second sense of Idetachi: eating at the time of departure. Pera is the printed historical Portuguese form; the physical row ends after pera and continues with fora below.

Fora completes the departure phrase. The upright examples Idetachiuo ſuru and furumǒ concern taking or providing the departure meal. The intervening alternative marker l, is visibly slanted italic type; retain the caron in furumǒ.

runs.text: Comer quando hum vai pera fora. Na prati-

lines.note: The Portuguese explains eating when one goes away, then starts a usage comment. The printed hyphen in prati- joins ca in the next physical row; neither the explanation nor the word is a new entry.

runs.text: ca ſe vſa mais Detachi, u. Vt,

lines.note: The usage comment says the shorter Detachi, u. is more usual in speech. That mentioned Japanese form occurs inside the italic Portuguese explanation; the second, upright Detachi begins the example continued below.
Uo ſuru completes the preceding Japanese example, followed by italic &c. The small amount of text belongs to the same entry and is retained as its own physical continuation row.

Cotonaru tçuchi and Tacocu explain Ido as another land or kingdom. They are upright Japanese equivalents, not words embedded within Portuguese prose; Outro begins the Portuguese gloss continued below.
Reino completes Outro reino, another kingdom. The terminal S. is an upright usage label, not part of the italic Portuguese definition; it is kept outside the italic span.

This homographic Ido means the place where someone is. The example Idouo ta- continues on the next row; retain the printed grave in està and the visible line-end hyphen rather than completing the verb here.

Tçu completes the example meaning to leave one's place. The paragraph then begins Vo-ido, a separate women's-language use continued across the physical line break; neither fragment is a new headword row.

runs.text: Vſão as molheres por traſeira, ou

lines.note: Ido completes Vo-ido. The Portuguese explicitly attributes this respectful word for the rear or buttocks to women's usage; retain molheres and traſeira as printed rather than modernizing their spelling.

runs.text: poſteriores falando com reſpeito da peſſoa.

lines.note: The continuation specifies the posterior parts while speaking respectfully of the person. Peſſoa has the doubled long-s spelling; the sentence and this homographic sense end on this physical row.

This Ido is a water well, with the upright alternative inomoto. The scan has the initial i followed by n, not the draft's momoto; the Portuguese reads Poço without the draft's unsupported grave accent. Retain the comma after Ido and the alternative marker l,.

Cuſuxino michi identifies Idǒ as the art of medicine. The headword has a V-shaped caron in this impression; preserve it rather than regularizing the vowel to the circumflex found in other long-vowel forms.
The example is a person accomplished in medicine. The mark in Idǒno matches the caron of the preceding headword, not the draft's circumflex. Fiſica here denotes medicine, not modern physics.
The left edge shows capital I followed by docoro, not Adocoro. The Portuguese defines a place where someone is; retain the printed grave in eſtà and the source form hum.

Idori is glossed sitting; the upright inflectional series u, otta is distinct from the definition. Yuru- begins the example adverb carried into the next physical row, with the printed hyphen retained.
Rito completes Yururito, and idoru completes the example of sitting at ease. The Portuguese explanation continues onto vontade below; retain aßentado and the grave in à.
Vontade completes the expression for being very much at one's ease. The X. is an upright register label; the draft's isolated italic full stop is corrected to belong with that label.

runs.text: Roſeiras que dão hũas roſas brancas

lines.note: The consonant after the first o is r, not the draft's t: Idoro names rose bushes bearing white roses. The Portuguese description remains open and continues with cheiroſas below; no terminal punctuation is supplied.

runs.text: cheiroſas. X. No Cami ſe diz ibara.

lines.note: The roses are fragrant, and an upright X. precedes the regional usage comment. Cami and ibara are Japanese names mentioned inside the Portuguese explanation, both in its italic type. Separate the tightly set Cami ſe; enlargement identifies the short initial of ibara as lowercase i with an offset dot, not l or capital I.

Idǒxa is glossed Medico, a physician, and ends the D subdivision before the following section heading. Preserve the caron visible above the headword vowel rather than normalizing its long-vowel notation.

The new F subdivision starts with a two-line enlarged I before Fai; the draft lost that initial. Tagai ſomuqu is the upright Japanese equivalent, and the Portuguese gives transgression before introducing the example on the following row.

Fattouo ifaiſuru exemplifies violating the law. Its horizontal displacement accommodates the preceding enlarged I rather than beginning a separate entry; the Portuguese retains the historical spelling ley.

runs.text: Hũa taboazinha em que eſtà eſcrito o no-

lines.note: A different Ifai is a small memorial tablet on which a dead person's name is written. Taboazinha and the grave in eſtà are retained; no- is the printed first part of nome at the row end.

runs.text: me de algum defunto diante da qual poẽ cha,

lines.note: Me completes nome. The description says tea is placed before the tablet; poẽ has its printed nasal abbreviation on e, and cha is Portuguese within the explanatory sentence, not a roman Japanese example or a font-toggle term.
Cooked rice and other offerings for the deceased complete the tablet description. Preserve the printed &c. and pera; the row is a continuation rather than a separate ritual headword.

runs.text: Lugar onde poem esta taboa que com-

lines.note: Ifaijo is the place where this tablet is set. The Portuguese begins the word commũmente as com- at the right edge, with its printed hyphen preserved for continuation below.

runs.text: mũmente he algũa capella, ou ermida onde

lines.note: Mũmente completes the preceding word. The usual location is described as a chapel or hermitage; retain the nasal marks in mũmente and algũa and the historical spellings he and capella.

runs.text: ſe enterra o de funto, ou pellomenos esta o

lines.note: The place contains the deceased's burial, or at least the written name. The visibly separated de funto is retained as printed spacing rather than silently joined to match other occurrences of defunto; pellomenos and esta remain unchanged.
Seu nome eſcrito finishes the qualification about a name recorded at the site. The short physical continuation ends in &c.; no text is merged with the next headword.

runs.text: Ifen. Tagai cauaru. i, Yacuſocuuo chiga-

lines.note: Ifen has the upright equivalents Tagai cauaru and Yacuſocuuo chiga-yuru, with the latter divided at the printed hyphen. The i, introduces a Japanese equivalent and is not italic Portuguese or a citation label.

runs.text: Quebrar o concerto, ou promeſſa. Vt,

lines.note: Yuru completes the Japanese equivalent divided above. The Portuguese gives breaking an agreement or promise, with concerto in its agreement sense; Vt, introduces the complete upright example on the following line.
Yacuſocuuo ifenſuru is the example for breaking a promise. This entire physical row is Japanese in upright type; no Portuguese explanation or embedded-word font toggle is added.

runs.text: Ifeô. l, ifiô. i, Yoni chigǒta coto.

lines.note: Ifeô and the alternative ifiô denote singularity or deviation from the ordinary, explained by Yoni chigǒta coto. The headword accents differ from the caron in chigǒta; retain these distinctions and the printed Singu- break.

Laridade completes Singularidade. The Portuguese describes discrepancy from the common or usual and introduces an example; commum is the printed historical spelling, not a transcription error to modernize.
The example Anofitoua ifeôuo tatçuru concerns a person acting in novel or unconventional ways. The explanatory Aquelle ho- is broken at the right edge with a visible hyphen and continues below.

Mem completes homem and the explanation says the man comes out with novelties. The next example has a visible circumflex in Ifeôuo, not the draft's caron; retain the abbreviation cõ and the paragraph division.
The gloss Ser amigo de nouidades explains the preceding example as being fond of novelties. The next upright phrase begins Ifeôna mo-; preserve its circumflex and printed final hyphen.
No completes mono, giving an unusual or extravagant person. The Portuguese gloss uses singular and extrauagante; the row completes the same headword's examples and is not independently reheaded.

runs.text: Pelle de hum animal que tem eſpinhos como

lines.note: The scan starts with capital I, not lowercase i. Ifi is first described as the skin of an animal with spines; the comparison continues below, so no species identification beyond the dictionary's wording is imposed.

runs.text: ouriço cacheiro. ¶ Itẽ, O meſmo animal.

lines.note: The animal is compared with an ouriço cacheiro, and the paragraph adds that the word also names the animal itself. Retain the printed nasal abbreviation Itẽ and the paragraph sign.

The entire Ifô headword is upright, including its initial I and full stop; the draft's isolated italic characters are not supported. Cotonaru cuni is a Japanese equivalent meaning another country, followed by the Portuguese gloss another kingdom.

Ixano nori identifies the rules or precepts of medicine. The remaining mark above the headword o is a single acute-like stroke, so the diplomatic choice is Ifó; the supplied NINJAL index has Ifǒ, but does not establish a missing second stroke in this impression. The Portuguese reads fiſica, not the draft's ffica.

Yaſui nori explains this separate Ifô as an easy religious teaching or sect. Preserve the circumflex and the Portuguese characterization as easy and without effort; it is distinct from the medical entry above.

Cotonaru nori denotes a different teaching or sect, matching Outra ſeita differente. These upright Japanese words are an equivalent, not embedded Portuguese terms; the entry's original spelling and double f are retained.

Capital I and the caron over u are visible. This homograph denotes power and pomp or magnificence; retain fauſto as the historical Portuguese gloss rather than substituting a modern paraphrase in the text.
The next Ifǔ describes a foreign or rough custom through the Portuguese words barbaro and agreſte. This is a distinct homographic entry, not a continuation of the power-and-pomp sense above.

runs.text: Coſtumes que alguẽ deixou depois de mor-

lines.note: The third Ifǔ concerns customs left behind by someone after death. Preserve the nasal abbreviation alguẽ and the printed mor- division, whose final syllable begins the next physical row.

runs.text: to, quer ſejam bõs, ou maos.

lines.note: To completes morto. The explanation explicitly includes customs whether good or bad; bõs retains the printed nasal mark and maos the source's unaccented spelling.

The headword begins with capital I, not lowercase l, and is followed by the Japanese equivalent Nunogoromo. The stop after Ifu is extremely faint, so the aligned punctuation is conservatively retained; the Portuguese definition continues into canemo below.

Canemo completes the material description of the garment, referring to hemp or hempen cloth. Retain this historical form as one short physical continuation rather than combining the row with the headword above.
The leftmost letter is capital I and the headword is wholly upright. Ifucu is simply glossed clothing; this closes the F subdivision before the separate G heading.

An enlarged two-line I belongs before Gabacama at the beginning of the G subdivision. The Portuguese describes tight, narrow breeches; the visible word boundary is restored between Calçoẽs and apertados, while the explanation continues below.

The breeches are tight around the lower legs near the Tabis. Tabis is a Japanese clothing term mentioned within the italic Portuguese sentence and is eligible for the font-toggle map; it is not a standalone example.

The Japanese equivalent reads Ixano gacumon, with a visible x omitted by the draft. The Portuguese begins the definition as the study or science of medicine and continues on the following physical row.
Da medicina completes the gloss of Igacu. This short row belongs to the preceding entry, not to the next verb, and its italic setting is retained.
Igami is glossed the dog's whining or yelping. The inflected form is ǒda with a caron and the noun cão has a nasal mark; retain both printed distinctions.

runs.text: Sebe que esta ao derredor da Miya,

lines.note: Restore the left-edge capital I in Igaqi and read esta, not esti. The shrine word Miya has a clear i-dot and a very weak remaining stem, supporting Miya rather than the draft's Mya; it occurs inside Portuguese prose. The comma leads to the separate catchword ou below.
